what_it_does: Modern AI chips often have special hardware that accelerates structured sparsity — a pattern where, say, exactly 2 out of every 4 numbers in a weight matrix are zero (called 2:4 sparsity). This hardware is fast and energy-efficient, but only helps models that were specifically trained with that exact pattern. Models pruned with arbitrary (unstructured) sparsity cannot use it. TASD is a mathematical trick that re-expresses any sparse matrix as a short sum of structured-sparse matrices, so unstructured or fully dense models can run on structured-sparse hardware without any retraining.
method_in_detail:
The idea. Basic algebra says A x B = (A1 + A2) x B = A1 x B + A2 x B. If you can split matrix A into two matrices A1 and A2 that each obey the hardware's required pattern (say 4-out-of-8 non-zeros per block and 1-out-of-8 non-zeros per block), the hardware can process each piece efficiently and sum the results. The key insight is that even though the sum A1 + A2 might not follow any single structured pattern, each term individually does. TASD applies this decomposition greedily: at each step, extract the largest elements that fit the pattern into the next term and keep the residual for the next term.

How it works for weights (static). The TASDER software tool takes a pruned model, measures for each layer what fraction of non-zeros would be dropped by each possible decomposition, and greedily picks the most aggressive decomposition that still keeps model accuracy above 99% of the original. The resulting structured-sparse weight tensors are baked into the model once and run efficiently at inference time.

How it works for activations (dynamic). Activations change with every input, so decomposition must happen at runtime. A small TASD hardware unit sits at the output of each compute tile, inspects each block of values, pulls out the largest ones as the first structured term, and saves the residual for a second pass. Because the tile produces output faster than the TASD unit processes it, enough units are added (following Little's Law) to ensure no stalls.

The key design choice. Keeping the output partial-sum matrix C stationary in fast on-chip memory while rotating the decomposed A tiles through avoids expensive off-chip memory traffic for the accumulation, making the overhead of two sequential passes small.

The result. TASD improves energy-delay product (a combined measure of speed and power efficiency) by up to 83% across dense and sparse versions of ResNet50 and BERT, with no retraining required. On real NVIDIA RTX 3080 hardware with 2:4 sparse tensor cores (the GPU's dedicated math units), it achieves up to 39% runtime speedup.
